messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 59

He is 32, European, married, and works as a tutor, a job that once fit him well because it let him move between small conversations and concentrated, one-to-one work without much attention on himself. Before the stalking begins, he describes himself as steady, private, and reasonably confident in his routines. He spends long hours helping students prepare for exams, and he likes the quiet satisfaction of seeing someone understand a difficult idea. His life feels contained and predictable until a former acquaintance starts inserting himself into it in ways that first seem odd, then unsettling, and then impossible to ignore.

At the beginning, the contact is intermittent. A message that appears too late at night. A comment from a student about someone asking after him. A car he notices more than once near his home. He tries to account for each thing separately, telling himself he is being overly cautious, that he is reading too much into coincidence. He does not want to alarm his wife, and he does not want to become the sort of person who sees threats everywhere. For a while he continues working, meeting students in libraries and quiet cafés, while keeping a small part of his attention fixed on the street outside.

The pattern tightens over time. The man learns his schedule, appears in places he should not know about, and leaves messages that are not explicitly violent but feel unmistakably invasive. The patient begins to change the way he moves through the world. He checks locks more than once. He varies his route to work. He scans reflections in windows and the faces around him before he sits down anywhere. He stops taking calls from unfamiliar numbers and lets the phone ring out while his stomach knots. When he is tutoring, he finds himself losing focus halfway through an explanation because he is suddenly certain someone is outside the room. He apologizes to students, blames fatigue, and then is ashamed of how often his mind slips away from the lesson and into the possibility of being watched.

What unsettles him most is the way ordinary spaces become charged with threat. The front door, the train platform, the parking lot near the tutoring center, even the hallway outside his bedroom all begin to feel like sites of exposure. He starts sleeping lightly, waking at the smallest sound. He and his wife, who had once moved through the evening with an easy familiarity, now discuss practical details in low voices: where he will be, when he will be home, whether she should walk him to the car. He appreciates her concern and at the same time feels embarrassed by how dependent he becomes on reassurance. He notices himself becoming irritable when plans change at the last minute, not because the change matters in itself but because unpredictability feels dangerous.

After one particularly frightening incident, when he finds a note left in a place that suggests the stalker has been close to his home, he reports feeling a kind of collapse inside himself. The world does not feel secure enough to return to normal even after he takes the usual steps to protect himself. He checks doors, blinds, and mirrors repeatedly. He replays past encounters, trying to determine what he missed and whether he somehow invited the attention by being polite or not forceful enough. The self-questioning wears him down. He is often tense in his shoulders and jaw, and he describes a constant readiness, as if his body has learned to anticipate interruption even in quiet moments.

As months pass, he becomes more avoidant without fully intending to. He declines social invitations. He chooses the same familiar shops and the same narrow range of places where he can see exits clearly. He still tutors, but he limits the number of students he sees in person and sometimes arranges sessions online when he feels especially unsettled. Even then, he sits with his back to a wall and keeps his eyes flicking toward the doorway. He is not dramatic about what has happened; instead, he seems worn by the effort of managing it. He speaks of feeling “on guard” all the time, of being unable to relax even when nothing obvious is happening. At night, when the house is finally quiet, he lies awake listening for sounds that may or may not mean someone is near, and the silence itself no longer feels restful.
